title: To Begin the World Again
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/brooke-allen
text:
The name of Thomas Paine is far better known than the life of the man behind it. Yet Paine’s origins had everything to do with the democratic causes that inspired his unmatched brilliance as a popular communicator. Son of a Quaker corset maker, he hailed from Norfolk, a county swept up in the radically egalitarian Leveller movement that arose during the English Civil War less than a century before his birth, in 1737. Paine failed in brief careers as a corset maker, excise officer, schoolteacher, and tobacconist before concluding that the only possible life for him was one of writing and reflecting. He came to America on the eve of the Revolution, with a letter of introduction from Benjamin Franklin, whom he had met in London, and began what would quickly become a dazzling career as a pamphleteer, newspaper writer, and propagandist of genius: Common Sense (1776) made him perhaps the greatest “influencer” in our nation’s history. 

The success of the American Revolution having led him to suppose that the entire world was ripe for revolution and that all revolutions would follow the course of the American version, he moved to France in 1792 and took an active part in that rebellion before falling afoul of the radical Jacobins. A permanent exile from his native England, where he had been tried in absentia for seditious libel, Paine ended his days in the United States, where his egotism and garrulousness kept former friends at bay. He died, nearly penniless, in 1809. Still, for all that he accomplished in his seventy-two years, Paine’s reputation in America rests mainly on the two-word title of a forty-seven-page pamphlet he published in January 1776, itself a collection of polemical letters arguing for the separation of the American Colonies from Britain and the creation of an egalitarian democracy. 

Putting on the True Character of a Man

Common Sense: But was it? Is it? Certainly, Paine’s decision to heed his friend Benjamin Rush’s advice and rename his broadside (first given the working title Plain Truth) proved a stroke of publishing genius. The title itself invited readers of the best-selling work to accept its revolutionary propositions as nothing less than commonsensical—or at least to entertain the idea that they might be. Thomas Jefferson, the other great propagandist of the American Revolution, took a similar approach in his Declaration of Independence. As historian Gordon S. Wood has noted, Jefferson wrote in a letter to Henry Lee that his purpose in the Declaration was “not to find out new principles, or new arguments, never before thought of…; but to place before mankind the common sense of the subject; [in] terms so plain and firm as to command their assent, and to justify ourselves in the independent stand we [are] compelled to take.” Jefferson’s “common sense” was expressed in such confident, ringing tones that few of us have stopped to nitpick. We seldom bother considering which parts of the document were sensible and which were clearly not. 

As for Paine, consider how he began the section of Common Sense titled “Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs”:

In the following pages I offer nothing more than simple facts, plain arguments, and common sense: and have no other preliminaries to settle with the reader, than that he will divest himself of prejudice and prepossession, and suffer his reason and his feelings to determine for themselves: that he will put on, or rather that he will not put off, the true character of a man, and generously enlarge his views beyond the present day.

This is a simplified version of the Enlightenment project: Get rid of prejudices and preconceptions, and reason will lead you to truth. It had been the guiding principle of Enlightenment thinkers at least since John Locke, and Paine summed up a century of progressive thought in the sentence. He was persuasive, and he convinced his readers that he himself was writing without prejudice or preconception, though of course he had his own tenderly nurtured prejudices and preconceptions, as all of us do. Paine and Jefferson between them presented America with a national myth, or narrative, that has proved remarkably resilient despite the fact that so many of their predictions for the future of the nation have failed to come true. And we still cling to residues of that national narrative two and a half centuries later, when much that Paine hated about eighteenth-century Britain now blights the United States, including extreme social and economic inequality, compromised elections, abrogated rights, an overweening executive, unfettered warmongering, and imperial overreach, among other social and political ills.

There were enough judicious and clear-sighted statements in Common Sense to compel Paine’s original readers to accept his arguments in toto, but with hindsight one can clearly separate genuine common sense from wishful thinking and utopian fantasy. He was correct, for example, to say that America’s size and geographic distance from Britain presented a problem to the imperialists: “[T]here is something absurd,” Paine wrote, “in supposing a Continent to be perpetually governed by an island.” True. “Even the distance at which the Almighty hath placed England and America is a strong and natural proof that the authority of the one over the other, was never the design of Heaven.” Again, hard to argue with. But what follows is not: “As to government matters, ’tis not in the power of Britain to do this continent justice: the business of it will soon be too weighty and intricate to be managed with any tolerable degree of convenience, by a power so distant from us, and so very ignorant of us.” Yes, it would seem so—but Britain successfully administered Canada for nearly another century and cooperated peacefully in its eventual shift to self-government. 

Kings and Subjects

Paine’s arguments against the institution of monarchy have become something like Holy Writ in the United States, so much so that many Americans can righteously carry “No Kings” banners while conceding that representative democracy has hardly brought the cream to the top. Some of us would even prefer to be ruled by King Charles III—or George III, for that matter!—than by our brazenly imperious current president. “No Kings” is the American credo, and Paine’s diatribe did much to make it so. He railed against “the distinction of men into KINGS and SUBJECTS,” for which neither nature nor religion has given a plausible reason, and pointed to the unfitness of so many royal heirs as one of the “natural proofs of the folly of hereditary right in kings.” The ruling British dynasty originated, Paine said, in a “French bastard [William the Conqueror] landing with an armed Banditti.” He went on to fulminate against the foisting of hereditary monarchs upon later generations, asserting that hereditary succession was “an insult and imposition on posterity.” He continued: 
“[I]t is more than probable, that, could we take off the dark covering of antiquity and trace [monarchs] to their first rise, we should find the first of them nothing better than the principal ruffian of some restless gang.”

All very well, and most believers in representative government would agree with him, but Paine’s attempt to cast the particular monarch he was talking about, the hapless George III, as “the hardened, sullen-tempered Pharaoh of England” was patently absurd. As Andrew Roberts, George’s most recent biographer, has credibly demonstrated, the king was “as cultured, civilized, enlightened, and good-natured a monarch as it is possible to find in European history,” and while it is true that he engaged in a spirited power struggle at home with the emerging political “left”—the liberal wing of the Whig Party—he was content to work within the strictures imposed on a constitutional monarch by the settlement of 1688, and never sought a return to autocracy. Jefferson, too, knew that George was no tyrant, despite the hyperbolic language and exaggerated claims he made against him in the Declaration. If George had been an actual tyrant, the First and Second Continental Congresses would not have been permitted to assemble, and the ringleaders of the Revolution, including Paine, would have been arrested and probably hanged. The essential clemency of George and his ministers was even more evident during the Napoleonic Wars, after Paine had published the seditious Rights of Man and was openly encouraging England to have a revolution of its own. The policy of George III and William Pitt was not to punish Paine but simply to force him into permanent exile.

The Enlightenment Fallacy

Paine said some remarkably prescient things in Common Sense. The truth of one of his intuitions—that “it only remains to know which power in the constitution has the most weight, for that will govern”—plays out dramatically today, every time we open a newspaper or turn on the television. Common Sense is full of similarly shrewd and pithy observations, the combined effect of which suggests that such sagacity will prevail throughout the document. But then we come upon a number of fairly outlandish claims. “Where there are no distinctions,” Paine wrote, “there can be no superiority, perfect equality affords no temptation.” Even in 1776 this must have been a dubious proposition, but two hundred fifty years of representative government have demonstrated that perfect equality is impossibly utopian, even though formal equality before the law is a reasonable and sometimes achievable desideratum. As for banishing temptation, we are all too aware that there is no limit on people’s greed, or their lust for power. 

If there is an Enlightenment project—narrowly defined for our purposes as the rejection of prejudice and preconceptions and the embrace of reason as the guide to truth—it is in many ways an admirable one. But then there is also an Enlightenment fallacy—a great and potentially dangerous one—of which we should be ever cautious. The philosopher John Gray is worth quoting at length here:

The idea of evil as it appears in modern secular thought is an inheritance from Christianity. To be sure, rationalists have repudiated the idea; but it is not long before they find they cannot do without it. What has been understood as evil in the past, they insist, is error—a product of ignorance that human beings can overcome.… But how to account for the fact that humankind is deaf to the voice of reason? At this point rationalists invoke sinister interests—wicked priests, profiteers from superstition, malignant enemies of enlightenment, secular incarnations of the forces of evil.

As so often is the case, secular thinking follows a pattern dictated by religion while suppressing religion’s most valuable insights. Modern rationalists reject the idea of evil while being obsessed by it. Seeing themselves as embattled warriors in a struggle against darkness, it has not occurred to them to ask why humankind is so fond of the dark.

It is an illusion that informed at least a part of the Founding project. Those who embraced it most uncritically, Jefferson and Paine among them, spoke with more optimism—and hence with more popular effect—than those who did not, notably John Adams and James Madison. “Yes, we can” won the battle for hearts and minds because it provided, as it would in 2008, an active vision of hope, and because it conformed with positive ideas about human empathy introduced to American thought through the work of Scottish Enlightenment theorists such as Adam Smith, Adam Ferguson, and Francis Hutcheson. Hope is always a potent political message; indeed, inspirational leadership is hardly possible in its absence. And in 1789, the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (penned by the French Revolutionary leaders and influenced by Paine’s work) would repeat the Enlightenment fallacy in its very first sentence: “…considering that ignorance, neglect, or contempt of human rights, are the sole causes of public misfortunes and corruptions of Government….”

The sole causes? Really? Ignorance is certainly one of the principal causes of human folly, misery, and degradation, but hardly the only one. “Reason obeys itself,” Paine proclaimed in his great screed of 1791–1792, The Rights of Man, “and ignorance submits to whatever is dictated to it.” Again, it sounds good, but one can think of counterexamples, and some of the most highly educated people in the world have followed insane creeds as meekly as sheep. “Mankind, as it appears to me,” Paine asserted, also in The Rights of Man, “are always ripe enough to understand their true interest, provided it be presented clearly to their understanding, and that in a manner not to create suspicion by anything like self-design, nor offend by assuming too much.” It is hard to make this claim in the twenty-first century. How is “mankind” to decide which of the many voices clamoring to explain its “true interest” it should listen to? It was already difficult enough in Paine’s own time, with its proliferation of newspapers and pamphlets advancing competing agendas. In today’s fractured mediascape, it has become nearly impossible. And which of the many would-be explicators is free of “self-design”? 

The Declaration of Independence and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, published just thirteen years apart, marked a new epoch, one we still inhabit. The world has not been the same since they appeared; it cannot be. It is easy to deride their authors for not counting women or enslaved people among those created equal, but the documents inspired movements that led inevitably to the extension of rights to these excluded groups. 

The new world these texts created was built on a central foundation: that all men possess natural rights, rights Jefferson alleged to be unalienable. In The Rights of Man, Paine attempted to define this hazy concept:

Natural Rights are those which appertain to Man in right of his existence. Of this kind are all the intellectual rights, or rights of the mind: and also all those rights of acting as an individual, for his own comfort and happiness, which are not injurious to the Natural Rights of others.—Civil Rights are those which appertain to Man, in right of his being a member of society. Every Civil Right has for its foundation some Natural Right pre-existing in the individual…

Again, is this “common sense” or wishful thinking? No one has cared to admit it from that day to this, but there is good reason to doubt that “natural rights” actually exist. In practice, it may seem that they do only if those in power agree to govern in a way that affirms the existence and legitimacy of such rights. By such reasoning, if those in power are willing to respect what Enlightenment thinkers like Paine deemed “natural rights,” then we can delude ourselves into thinking that such rights exist; if the powerful do not acknowledge such rights, as in pre-Enlightenment kingdoms and empires, or, more recently, in totalitarian states, then, the skeptic might conclude, they do not exist. Rights are what those in power allow.

But in the years since Paine wrote, the idea of rights—and their legitimacy—has continued to evolve via something that might be called the climate of informed opinion: an amalgam of philosophical and religious precepts, some derived from reason and empirical observation, some from religious revelation (which Paine, a decrier of “revealed” religion, would have downplayed), and some from simple human empathy—the empathy that had been deemed an inextricable part of human nature by the Scottish Enlightenment thinkers as well as by Jean-Jacques Rousseau, one of the contemporary thinkers Paine read avidly. The Enlightenment thinkers who formulated the idea of natural rights based the idea on their belief in a deity, “Nature’s God” in Jefferson’s formulation, who, being benign (unlike the Old Testament Yahweh), endowed his creatures (human creatures only, though some sages, such as Rousseau, were already extending the idea to animals) with these rights. Today, fewer people are so sure about God; so where might our modern ideas of rights come from? Idealism, decency, goodwill, and even, according to evolutionary scientists, innate altruism—though these qualities are too often insufficient to limit greed or check the will to power.

The Rights of Man was written as a retort to Edmund Burke’s Reflections on the Revolution in France, which Paine saw as apostasy. Burke, a reliable ally on the left until that point (he had vocally opposed the repressive policies of the British government against the American colonists, for instance), had come out against the French Revolution and denounced the Declaration of the Rights of Man as “paltry and blurred shreds of paper about the rights of men.” This outraged Paine: “Does Mr. Burke mean to deny that man has any rights? If he does, then he must mean that there are no such things as rights anywhere, and that he has none himself… If Governments, as Mr. Burke asserts, are not founded on the Rights of MAN, and are founded on any rights at all, they consequently must be founded on the rights of something that is not man. What then is that something?” On order and convenience, one might posit, or on the need for the smooth and peaceful running of society. Paine and Burke were both right, and both wrong. Paine erred, as A.J. Ayer wrote, “in his consistently underestimating both the determination of monarchs and aristocrats to retain their privileges and the strength of the habit of obedience which secured them the loyalty even of those whom they oppressed.” Burke erred in not seeing that the monarchy he revered was doomed in a new world created by the Declaration of Independence and the Declaration of the Rights of Man. Only a century after Burke’s death, Britain’s Hanoverian-Windsor dynasty would be bled of its political power. But his cynicism about human nature and people’s willingness to be led was very often justified. Paine complained that Burke considered humankind “a herd of beings that must be governed by fraud, effigy, and show; and an idol would be as good a figure of monarchy with him, as a man.” Was he wrong?

Public Coffers and the Pursuit of Happiness

Paine’s finest moment, I think, comes in Part II of The Rights of Man and Part I of his 1797 pamphlet Agrarian Justice, in which, greatly ahead of his time, he laid out what in effect was a social welfare state. “When, in countries that are called civilized,” he writes, “we see age going to the workhouse and youth to the gallows, something must be wrong in the system of Government.” There may no longer be workhouses or gallows, but gaping social and economic injustices endure and seem to have grown worse in recent years. Paine went on: “…[T]here lies hidden from the eye of common observation, a mass of wretchedness that has scarcely any other chance, than to expire in poverty or infamy. Its entrance into life is marked with the presage of its fate; and until this is remedied, it is vain to punish.” Again, has anything changed? And why have two hundred fifty years of representative government, which was supposed to “explode ignorance and preclude imposition,” not revealed to us the humanity of our fellow beings?

Those who complain about lazy welfare recipients or “welfare queens” might consider Paine’s insistence that “[p]ublic money ought to be touched with the most scrupulous consciousness of honour. It is not the produce of riches only, but of the hard earnings of labour and poverty.” Such scruples have seldom troubled modern presidents and lawmakers; even self-styled “conservative” governments that claim to oppose government waste have treated the public coffers as their own piggy banks. The disastrous invasion and occupation of Iraq, for instance, cost—after adjustment for inflation—thirteen times as much as the entire Marshall Plan: two trillion dollars that would have more than paid for every social welfare expense of the sort that Paine proposed. Social security, he said, “is not of the nature of a charity, but of a right.” So, he insisted, is education, because a nation “under a well-regulated Government, should permit none to remain uninstructed. It is Monarchical and Aristocratical Government only that requires ignorance for its support.” He proposed modest sums for newly married couples, for young people setting out in the world, and even for funeral expenses. The elderly would receive a pension. He advocated progressive, but not onerous, taxation. He called for a sort of Works Progress Administration avant la lettre. He insisted on the freedom of workmen to bargain. His program is in fact very close to what the British Labour government introduced in 1945. There is no mention of health care, probably because no system of health care existed in his day, and because eighteenth-century health care was primitive and not very effective.

When it shall be said in any country in the world, my poor are happy; neither ignorance nor distress is to be found among them; my jails are empty of prisoners, my streets of beggars; the aged are not in want, the taxes are not oppressive; the rational world is my friend, because I am the friend of its happiness. When these things can be said, then may that country boast its Constitution and its Government.

It hardly needs to be pointed out that we, as a society, are far from having fulfilled these conditions. Bernie Sanders still beats the same drum Paine did two and a half centuries on, and with about as much success. “If systems of Government can be introduced,” Paine believed, “less expensive, and more productive of general happiness, than those which have existed, all attempts to oppose their progress will, in the end, be fruitless. Reason, like time, will make its own way, and prejudice will fall in a combat with interest.” How wrong could anyone so intelligent be? It was the Enlightenment fallacy again. However much one wants to go along with the idealistic Paine, the old cynics too often seem correct. “[O]ur prejudices are our mistresses,” as Paine’s older contemporary, the Earl of Chesterfield, quipped; “reason is at best our wife, very often heard indeed, but seldom minded.”

Paine wagered all on the virtue and success of the French Revolution, moving to Paris in 1792 and taking a seat in the National Convention; he ended up languishing in the Luxembourg Palace prison during the Terror, witnessing personally the way leveling revolutions end up consuming their own champions. All of Burke’s forebodings about the Revolution had come to pass. In America, too, things did not go as Paine had been so confident they would. Dying in 1809, he lived long enough to see the nation head in a disturbing direction: Enlightened republicanism had ushered in not equality and virtue but a dog-eat-dog society of competitive and radical individualism. As Alexander Hamilton commented, “We may preach till we are tired of the theme, the necessity of disinterestedness in republics, without making a single proselyte.” 

It was not at all what the Founders had planned, and the abandonment of republican idealism continues today. The rise of our oligarchy would have appalled Paine. So, too, would the ignorance of the general public, Paine having believed that the “ignorant mob” was a product of the bad old regimes of Europe and would disappear under representative government. He would never have imagined that the sort of self-serving grifters we now routinely see in high government positions could ever be elected. He had been incensed when the Abbé Sieyès suggested that elected leaders tended to be worse than princely ones. “Such a mode of reasoning on such a subject is inadmissible,” he clucked, “because it finally amounts to an accusation upon Providence, as if she had left to man no other choice with respect to Government than between two evils.” Paine’s faith in “Providence” is touching, but a historical comparison between monarchs and elected leaders does not indicate a general superiority of one group over the other.

“We have it in our power to begin the world over again,” Paine proclaimed at the end of Common Sense. “A situation, similar to the present, hath not happened since the days of Noah until now. The birthday of a new world is at hand.” He was right, but there were no new-model humans to populate the new world, only the same old flawed, imperfectible animals. Two hundred fifty years later, politicians, newscasters, schoolteachers, and historians persist, sometimes all too wistfully, in calling America a shining city on a hill or the last best hope of mankind. In the end, though, our nation can only be as virtuous as the all-too-human material it is made of.
